case_name: V. Sumitra Reddy & Anr. v. K. Ranganadha Reddy & Ors.
holding_summary: In a dispute over a partnership at will (M/s Viraj Constructions, a railway-construction firm formed in 1964), the Supreme Court held that an outgoing partner's proportionate share in the dissolved firm's assets must be valued close to the date of actual settlement or sale, not frozen at the historical date of dissolution. The Court also held that a reconstituted firm has no right to use the dissolved firm's assets in the interim without first settling accounts with the outgoing partner, upholding a 25% share in the present value of the property and ordering a public auction where the partners fail to settle accounts themselves.
why_it_matters: Outgoing partners in a dissolved partnership are entitled to have their share valued at current, not historical, values — a significant financial protection where dissolution and final accounting are separated by years or decades, as is common in long-running family or construction partnerships.

case_name: Columbia Pictures Industries, Inc. v. Registrar of Trade Marks
holding_summary: Columbia Pictures, proprietor of the GHOSTBUSTERS mark in four classes, appealed the Registrar's rejection of its opposition to a third party's application to register GHOST BUSTER in Class 5 (pharmaceuticals). The Delhi High Court held that an earlier mark need not first have been formally declared 'well-known' under Sections 11(6)-(9) of the Trade Marks Act before its proprietor can invoke the cross-category protection under Section 11(2), and found GHOST BUSTER's adoption in an unrelated class would take unfair advantage of GHOSTBUSTERS' distinctive character and repute.
why_it_matters: This is now a second Delhi High Court ruling in 2026 (after Zara v. Zora) confirming that a proprietor can invoke Section 11(2) cross-class protection for a globally recognised mark without a prior formal well-known declaration, reinforcing a clear evidentiary route for brand owners defending against unrelated-class squatting.

citation: Notified 9 September 2026, Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution
court: Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (Government of India)
holding_summary: The Central Government notified the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026, amending the 2020 Rules to formally integrate the 2023 Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns into binding law, requiring e-commerce entities to conduct an annual self-audit and display a compliance certificate. The amendment overhauls algorithmic ranking rules, bans misleading search manipulation, mandates sponsored-listing disclosure, tightens grievance timelines to 48-hour acknowledgment and 30-day resolution, and requires sellers to disclose fuller product and transaction details including country of origin and return-shipping costs. The Rules take effect on 1 January 2027.
why_it_matters: E-commerce marketplaces and sellers have a defined runway to January 2027 to build dark-pattern self-audit processes, revise ranking algorithms and update seller disclosures — non-compliance from that date will be a binding regulatory breach rather than a voluntary guideline lapse.

case_name: Tata Projects Limited v. National Highways Authority of India
holding_summary: The Allahabad High Court quashed NHAI's mid-term termination of Tata Projects' Rs. 940.68 crore EPC contract for widening NH-709A, holding that NHAI's action was arbitrary and violated Article 14 of the Constitution. The Court held that the existence of an arbitration clause in the contract does not preclude the exercise of writ jurisdiction where a State authority acts arbitrarily in terminating a public contract, and that a High Court may intervene where the impugned termination is demonstrably arbitrary rather than a good-faith exercise of a contractual termination right.
why_it_matters: EPC contractors facing an arbitrary mid-term termination by a state authority like NHAI are not confined to arbitration alone — a writ petition remains available where the termination itself is shown to be arbitrary, giving contractors a faster interim route than a full arbitral reference.

case_name: K.K. Bansal v. Koninklijke Philips Electronics N.V.
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices C. Hari Shankar and Om Prakash Shukla set aside a 2018 single-judge decree that had directed two small DVD player makers to pay FRAND royalty to Philips for alleged infringement of a Standard Essential Patent covering DVD decoding technology. In a 150-page judgment, the Court held that Philips failed to prove the essentiality of the patent (IN-184753) and failed to establish infringement based on admissible evidence, and further held that the Bansals' acquisition of the patented components from market-authorised dealers constituted exhaustion of Philips' patent rights under Section 107A(b) of the Patents Act, 1970.
why_it_matters: SEP holders must independently prove essentiality and infringement with admissible evidence rather than relying on assumptions carried over from earlier proceedings, and downstream assemblers who source components from authorised dealers have a strong patent-exhaustion defence against royalty claims on those components.

case_name: New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) v. Rajveer Singh & Ors.
citation: Civil Appeal arising out of SLP (C) No. 18801 of 2025
holding_summary: In a land acquisition matter concerning an award passed on 15 February 1977, where connected first appeals concerning the same notification were decided by the High Court on different dates (8 July 2019 and 18 April 2022), a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran held that successive High Court orders in first appeals do not confer a fresh cause of action or extend the three-month limitation period for landowners to seek redetermination of compensation under Section 28A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The Court allowed NOIDA's appeal and rejected the landowners' Section 28A application as time-barred.
why_it_matters: Landowners seeking enhanced compensation under Section 28A after a connected first appeal enhances compensation for similarly placed land must file within three months of the original Reference Court award — a later, unrelated appellate order on the same notification does not reset that limitation clock.

case_name: SAP India Private Limited v. Cox & Kings Limited
holding_summary: The Justice Madan Lokur-led arbitral tribunal, constituted by the Supreme Court in January 2019, had adjourned SAP's Rs. 17.98 crore claim against Cox & Kings sine die after Cox & Kings entered CIRP in October 2019. After SAP sought resumption in February 2026, Justice Arif S. Doctor of the Bombay High Court extended the tribunal's mandate by one year and allowed the arbitration to proceed, holding that the delay in completing the arbitration was not attributable to any deliberate, wilful or negligent default by SAP or the tribunal.
why_it_matters: Claimants whose arbitration was genuinely and unavoidably stalled by the respondent's insolvency proceedings can secure a mandate extension years later without their claim being treated as abandoned, provided the delay is not of their own making.

case_name: Dharma Productions Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
holding_summary: Dharma Productions and Dharmatic Entertainment challenged GST demands totalling over ₹79.7 crore for FY 2017-18 to 2020-21, where tax authorities had classified their licensing of copyright in cinematographic films as licensing of 'information technology software' under SAC 998340, attracting 18% GST. A Division Bench of Justices M.S. Karnik and Sandesh D. Patil held that a cinematographic film — a passive audio-visual work incapable of execution, manipulation or interactivity — cannot satisfy the statutory definition of 'information technology software' merely because it is delivered digitally, and quashed the assessment and appellate orders.
why_it_matters: Confirms that the mode of digital delivery cannot itself reclassify content for GST purposes, protecting film producers, OTT licensors and other digital-content businesses from being taxed at software rates or under software classification codes for licensing audio-visual works.
